Sample text:
---
I'd like to write about alphabetical order, which I think is one of the strangest things humans have kept.

The order of the letters means nothing. No principle puts B after A or M before N, since the sequence isn't sorted by sound, shape, or frequency. Yet it is more than three thousand years old. Clay tablets from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BCE, list the letters of the local alphabet in an order that is recognizably ours: the sounds for a, b, g, and d near the start, k, l, m, n clustered in the middle, q, r, and t toward the end. The tablets were probably school exercises. Children were memorizing the sequence then for the same reason they do now, which is that someone older told them to.

From there the order passed through Phoenician, Greek, Etruscan, and Latin, and each handoff left small scars. My favorite involves G. The early Romans inherited the Greek zeta in seventh position, had no use for it, and dropped it. Later they wanted a letter to distinguish the hard g sound from k, since C had been doing both jobs. They made one by adding a stroke to C, and rather than put the new letter at the end, they gave it zeta's empty seat. A couple of centuries after that, Rome was absorbing Greek vocabulary and needed Z again. It was let back in, but its place was taken, so it went to the end of the line, where it still sits.

For most of this history, almost nobody used the order to organize anything. It was a way to teach the letters and little more. Medieval scholars who compiled reference works generally preferred arrangements that reflected the structure of the world: God before angels, angels before men, men before beasts. Sorting by spelling put "abbot" ahead of "angel" for no reason at all, and that looked like a refusal to think.

The alphabetical habit took centuries to spread. When Robert Cawdrey published an early English dictionary in 1604, he still felt he had to tell readers that they must learn "the order of the Letters as they stand," and he explained that b is near the beginning, n about the middle, and t toward the end.

I think the medieval scholars were right about what alphabetical order is and wrong about what it's worth. It is mindless, and that turned out to be its use. An arrangement by meaning only works if you already understand the subject and share the compiler's view of it. To find "whale" in such a book, you need to know whether the author considers it a fish. An arrangement by spelling asks only that you can spell, so a stranger to the field can use the book as easily as an expert can.

The same emptiness probably explains why the sequence lasted. Calendars were reformed because they drifted against the sun, and units of measure were standardized because trade demanded it. The order of the letters claims nothing about the world, so no discovery could ever show it to be wrong, and no one has had grounds to fix it.

So a child singing the alphabet song today is reciting, in slightly altered form, a Bronze Age school exercise. G comes seventh because the Romans had a vacancy, and Z comes last because it returned late.
---

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A polished, thesis-driven essay that turns a historical curiosity into a clear argument about the practical value of arbitrary systems.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and lightly conversational, using small historical details—especially G’s borrowed “empty seat”—to make an abstract point memorable. Its central turn is that alphabetical order’s apparent mindlessness makes it useful: it lets people find information without first sharing an expert’s worldview. The closing image of a child repeating an ancient school exercise gives the argument a quiet sense of continuity and invites the reader to notice the strange persistence of everyday conventions.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds alphabetical order as an arbitrary but durable human convention, tracing its history through teaching, scholarship, and reference works. It emphasizes accessibility over conceptual elegance, and suggests that a system can be valuable precisely because it claims nothing about the world.

## Evidence line
> It is mindless, and that turned out to be its use.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a coherent interest in how arbitrary conventions acquire practical value, though its polished explanatory style is not highly distinctive.
